paragraphs.heading: A flat shelf of rock
paragraphs.text: A wave-cut platform is a narrow, flat strip carved by erosion, often at the foot of a sea cliff or along the edge of a lake, bay or sea. It also goes by the names shore platform and coastal bench. These platforms tend to show best at low tide, when they appear as broad stretches of flat rock. Sometimes sand covers the landward part and forms a beach, and then the platform can only be seen at low tide or after storms shift the sand.

paragraphs.heading: From notch to cave to platform
paragraphs.text: A platform starts as a notch. Destructive waves beating on a cliff undercut it between the high and low water marks, mostly through abrasion, corrosion and hydraulic action, and this wave-cut notch grows into a cave. In time the cave roof can no longer hold, weakened by pressure and by freeze-thaw or biological weathering, and it falls in, so the cliff moves back inland. The cave floor is left behind as the platform. The fallen rock is ground into smaller pieces by attrition or washed out to sea, where some may settle at the platform's edge as an offshore beach.

paragraphs.heading: A record of old sea levels
paragraphs.text: Constant pounding by waves makes the platform a harsh home, and only certain organisms can use it. Old platforms record where sea and lake levels once stood, and raised, abandoned ones, sometimes found behind today's beaches, show that the sea was higher in the geological past. Dating them, or studying marine fossils on them, tells scientists when they formed and so where the sea stood at that time. In the United Kingdom and other once-glaciated areas this has been used to work out how fast land is rising now that its ice is gone. On coasts moved by earthquakes, a series of platforms can show earlier sea levels and how much each quake lifted the land.

paragraphs.heading: An argument over the name
paragraphs.text: Some researchers, including Trenhaile, Sunamura, and Massalink and Hughes, say the name wave-cut platform should be dropped. Their point is that the name assumes waves made the platform, and that is not always true. Shore platforms are erosional features, much like similar platforms along rivers and lakes. They form when waves and currents strip away saprock and other debris and leave a bare bedrock surface below the water table.
